intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 7 units · geology to population · drawn for a phone
This book is not “world geography” — it is **Eritrea**. Outcomes: read the land’s story (rocks), water, climate, plants and animals, soils, how people make a living, and who lives where.

intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: Based on Geography for Grade 12, Ministry of Education, Eritrea (2011). Sketch maps are teaching diagrams, not survey maps.

cards.title: Farming
body: Still the backbone: rain-fed cereals on the plateau, pastoralism in lowlands, some irrigation where water can be stored. Limited by rainfall deficit and soil loss.

cards.title: 6.1.1 Crop Production
body: A variety of crops can be grown in Eritrea due to the country’s diversity in climate and relief.
Crop production has historically been practiced in the highland regions.
Eritrean farmers traditionally cultivate cereal grains, legumes, fruits, and vegetables.
Farmers also raise goats, cattle, sheep, camels, donkeys, horses, and poultry.

cards.title: 6.1.2 Livestock Production
body: The great majority of the people in the Lowland regions of Eritrea depend on livestock.
Livestock play an important part in the economic lives of these communities.
Eritrea is endowed with large number of livestock.
The most densely populated Zobas –Maekel and Debubhave the lowest number of cattle.

cards.title: 6.1.3 Fishing
body: Fishing is a less developed economic sector in Eritrea but potentially one of the most profitable economic activities.
The Red Sea is home to more than 1,000 species of fish.
At present, fish consumption is relatively low, apart from Asmara and coastal areas.
Improved refrigeration and transport facilities are expected to increase fish consumption at a national level.

cards.title: 6.2 Manufacturing Industry
body: Prior to the introduction of modern industries in Eritrea, the material needs of the people were produced by local artisans in cottage industries.
In the 1940s and 1950s, Eritrea had a highly developed industrial base by the standard of other African colonies of the time.
The objectives of Italy’s colonial rule in Eritrea were to make the country (a) a source of market for its finished products, (b) a source of raw material for its industries.
The Italians established factories to produce consumer goods for their nationals in Eritrea.
Very few Eritreans were able to enter the commercial center as it continued to be dominated by foreign merchants, including Europeans, Indians and Yemeni businessmen.

**Step 1: Match crop requirements to altitude**
* Sesame: Lowlands ($$<1000\text{ m}$$).

Historical Background of Transport in Eritrea Modern transport began in Eritrea during the Italian colonial period.
The main objectives were to (a)link the ports with the hinterland.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Currently ________ mode of transportation is **commonly** used in Eritrea.
cards.why: In Eritrea, road transport is the most dominant and commonly used mode for both passenger travel and freight distribution. While air and water transport exist, they are specialized, and the railway is currently limited in its daily commercial scope.

cards.title: Energy & mining
body: Wood / biomass still common (deforestation risk). Alternatives: geothermal (Alid / rift), biogas from dung, wind (S. Red Sea, Dekemhare corridor). Minerals: gold and others known since Italian times; sector still developing.

cards.title: 6.4.1 Energy
body: In Eritrea, the most common sources of energy are biomass, oil products, electricity, and solar energy.
Of these, the largest proportion of total energy consumption is provided by biomass followed by petroleum.
Petroleum is used mainly as fuel for transportation, electricity generation and industrial production.
In Eritrea, exploration of oil and natural gas has been going on since the Italian period.

cards.title: 6.4.2 Mining
body: The mineral wealth of Eritrea has not been studied in detail.
The mining sector of Eritrea reached its climax between 1937 and 1939, when Italian colonial power exploited minerals such as gold, manganese and iron.
During the British Administration, all mines were closed down.
During Haileselassie’s time, mineral reserves such as copper were proven to exist.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: What proportion of total energy consumption in Eritrea is provided by traditional biomass sources?

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the energy sources used in Eritrea**
Traditional biomass energy sources (firewood, charcoal, dung and crop residues) account for about three-fourths ($$75\%$$) of the total energy consumption in the country.
The proportion is $$75\%$$ — which is why deforestation and the search for alternatives (solar, wind, geothermal, biogas) matter so much.

cards.title: Tourism
body: **Tourism** assets: highland architecture, Red Sea islands and diving, Danakil landscapes, cultural festivals — needs conservation so the attraction survives.

cards.title: 6.5.1 Natural Sites
body: In few hours time, a tourist can ascend from the hot beaches of the coast to the moderate weather of the Highlands.
The land surface of Eritrea also magnificent mountain scenery, traditional villages, and ancient archeological sites.

cards.title: 6.5.2 Historical Sites
body: Eritrea’s history is as old as humanity.
Numerous Italian-period buildings can be seen in Asmara, Keren, Dekemhare, and elsewhere.
The country is blessed with one of the highest numbers of ancient archeological sites in Africa outside of the Nile Valley.
The historical sites of the country include those located at Adulis Cohaito, Keskese, Tekhond’e, Metera and Der’at.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In which geological zone of Eritrea are rich deposits of gold, copper, zinc, and premium-quality marble concentrated?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Map minerals to geological regions**
The ancient Precambrian crystalline rocks hosting gold, base metals (copper, zinc), and high-grade construction marble are located in the Central and Northern Highlands.

**Step 2: Conclude**
The correct zone is the Central and Northern Highlands.

glossary.meaning: Biogas: This is an alternative source of energy to wood.
Agriculture is the primary source of income and food for the majority of the population in Eritrea.
Fishing is a less developed economic sector in Eritrea but potentially one of the most profitable economic activities.
Transport is the movement of people and goods.
Eritrea is a new nation in ancient land that offers rich archaeological sites that encourage tourists.

tips.text: Eritrea’s economy is primarily based on agriculture.
The country possesses vast arable land, for both rain fed and irrigated agriculture, but only a small portion is under cultivation.
Farming is traditional in its character and is meant for subsistence use.
As in all other economic sectors, the country’s transport infrastructure had been damaged badly due to the long war for independence.

Since independence, substantial work has been done to improve transport and communication infrastructure of the country. Similarly, industries were operating at a very low capacity because of inadequate technology and lack of supplies of raw materials.
The present pattern of energy consumption in Eritrea is not sustainable because it depends on the burning of biomass resources.

Efforts are underway to increase energy efficiency and to promote energy conservation. There are excellent opportunities for tourism industry in Eritrea because of its rich cultural heritage and magnificent landscapes.
However, the sector requires large investment and improved infrastructure.
Farming: Still the backbone: rain-fed cereals on the plateau, pastoralism in lowlands, some irrigation where water can be stored. Limited by rainfall deficit and soil loss.
Industry: Mostly light / processing near towns. Needs power, transport and raw materials.
Transport: Roads link highlands to ports (Massawa, Assab). Rail heritage Asmara–Massawa. Ports are the Red Sea door.

questions.q: During which colonial rule did Eritrea's economy substantially transform?
why: During the Italian colonial period (1890–1941) the Italians built factories (their number grew rapidly), roads, railways and ports; in the 1940s–50s Eritrea had a highly developed industrial base by African colonial standards – 'a radical transformation in terms of urbanization and industrialization'.
The British weakened the economy and the industrial sector declined after Ethiopia's occupation.

questions.q: The most important regions for agriculture in Eritrea include

options.D: Eastern Lowlands and South Eastern Highlands.

why:
**Step 1: Analyze agricultural zones.** Eritrea's agriculture is divided into rain-fed highland farming and commercial/irrigated lowland farming.
**Step 2: Identify key areas.** The **Central Highlands** (Maekel/Debub) are the heart of traditional rain-fed cereal production. The **South-Western Lowlands** (Gash-Barka) are known as the 'breadbasket' due to vast fertile plains and irrigation potential (e.g., Aligider, Teseney).
**Step 3: Match with options.** Option E correctly identifies these two primary zones.

questions.q: Mixed farming is when farmers grow crops and rear animals simultaneously. In Eritrea, this type of farming is highly practiced in the
why: In the **highland region** of Eritrea, farmers typically practice mixed farming on small, fragmented plots of land, where they grow food crops (like teff and barley) and keep a few livestock (like oxen and goats) for draft power and food.
